indian-startups-21cbafb622.headline: Nuclear startup Bluecore Energy raises $50M seed round, just two months after launch
indian-startups-21cbafb622.fulltext:
Bluecore Energy announced Tuesday an oversubscribed $50 million seed round — just months after raising a $10 million pre-seed and coming out of stealth.
As TechCrunch previously reported, the company, founded earlier this year by Kofi Asante, builds small nuclear reactors (SMRs) on floating barges, rather than fixed locations, to generate clean energy for ports and nearby infrastructure. This means that energy can be transported to wherever it is needed, an idea Asante hopes can bring clean power to those who need it most.
“The Navy is doing this as we speak, for the last 70 years, and has never had an accident,” Asante said about the use of portable technology in a new interview with TechCrunch. “We just made it smaller, so you can actually move things around in a way that doesn’t take years” — or a new set of infrastructure — ”but days.”
Asante wasn’t planning on fundraising this year, but calls kept coming after their pre-seed launch. Many of their pre-seed investors, including Slauson & Co., Harlem Capital, and Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen, doubled down on this new round, with new capital coming from investors like Collab Capital, Kevin Hart’s HartBeat Ventures, and angel investors from Tesla, Uber, Amazon, and Google. Silverton Partners led this new seed round, and it took eight weeks to close.
“I just kept having to figure out a way to make more room” — on the cap table, Asante said. “I wasn’t anticipating us raising that level of capital in that period of time, but really fortunate that we have so many investors and partners who are excited.”
When it emerged from stealth in July, it became the first nuclear company headquartered at a major port: the Port of Long Beach. It has since launched two floating barges and has struck a partnership with the Department of Transportation Maritime Division, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), and the U.S. Coast Guard. Bluecore Energy is now undergoing review with the NRC and the Coast Guard on its product design, which, if successful, will lead to certification of its floating nuclear power plant.
“We have been talking to them both since the inception of the company and design, but officially started the formal engagement in August,” Asante said.
The fresh capital will fund continued product development, regulatory work, nuclear fuel purchases, and hiring. Asante anticipates the biggest challenge to be the supply chain, securing hardware to build the right portable electricity infrastructure at a pace that can match consumer demand. He said that Bluecore Energy has seen inbound interest from “multiple ports, AI data centers and communities that need clean energy and water.”
“Our team comes from SpaceX, Rivian, and Toyota, so we are applying similar strategies to be able to secure critical parts,” he said. “We already have barges and a reactor and are now about to order nuclear fuel to go to our partner at a national nuclear lab.”
It all goes back to the core mission, Asante said, “to democratize access to clean energy.”
“My philosophy is that access to clean energy and also clean water should be a human right,” he said.

india-deep-tech-a4a3b53a0d.headline: Indian space startup GalaxEye wins US patent for Earth observation tech
india-deep-tech-a4a3b53a0d.fulltext:
Indian space startup GalaxEye wins US patent for Earth observation tech
The technology could allow satellites to capture clearer, more useful images, peering even through clouds, in all kinds of weather.
Indian space-tech startup GalaxEye has secured a US patent for a technology that could change the way satellites observe Earth, by bringing two very different kinds of imaging together on the same satellite.
The Bengaluru-based company said the patent covers a system that synchronises optical and radar sensors so they can capture precisely aligned images of the same location at the same time.
The technology is at the heart of GalaxEye’s OptoSAR imaging system.
The achievement comes as demand for satellite-based information grows across areas such as security, agriculture, insurance and disaster response.
The global commercial satellite imaging market was worth $6.55 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $20.15 billion by 2033, according to SkyQuest Technology.
ONE SATELLITE, TWO WAYS OF SEEING EARTH
The idea behind the OptoSAR technology is relatively simple.
Optical sensors work like sophisticated cameras, producing images that are easy to understand and revealing details such as vegetation, roads, buildings and water bodies.
But they depend on light and can also be blocked by clouds.
Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), on the other hand, uses microwave signals to observe the ground, operating during both day and night and seeing through cloud cover. This makes it a useful tool when optical cameras cannot get a clear view.
The challenge has traditionally been bringing these two types of information together.
Data collected from different satellites can come from different angles or at different times, making comparisons less precise.
GalaxEye’s patented architecture is designed to solve that problem by synchronising the sensors on a single platform, producing spatially and time-aligned observations.
"This patented technology enables us to serve the global markets and provide weather-agnostic imaging capabilities across sectors," CEO Suyash Singh told news agency Reuters.
A CONSTELLATION OF 30 SATELLITES
GalaxEye, founded by engineers from IIT Madras, took the technology into space with Mission Drishti, launched on May 3, 2026.
The company described it as the world's first OptoSAR satellite, while the Indian government also recognised it as the world's first satellite combining optical cameras and all-weather radar.
The mission, however, suffered a setback in July when GalaxEye lost communication with Drishti following an anomaly associated with a geomagnetic solar storm.
The company said the mission had nevertheless validated key spacecraft systems before the loss of contact.
GalaxEye now plans to build a 30-satellite constellation over the next five years, especially after also acquiring Bengaluru-based spacecraft engineering firm StarOps in August to strengthen its in-house capabilities.
The US patent gives the startup intellectual-property protection as it attempts to turn its Indian-developed technology into a global Earth-observation business.
India's own space economy is projected to grow to about $44 billion by 2033, according to the government's space-sector strategy, and this development is a step towards making that projection a reality.

india-deep-tech-f222eccebc.headline: Indian startup Agnikul Cosmos unveils testing & manufacturing hubs in Chennai to validate reusable rocket
india-deep-tech-f222eccebc.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: In a giant step towards attaining reusable launch vehicle technology like Elon Musk's 
SpaceX
, Indian space startup Agnikul Cosmos has inaugurated two new assembly and testing facilities in Chennai.
The company unveiled the Stage Testing & Inspection Facility (STIF) and the Pressurant Tank Realisation, Over-wrapping and Outfitting Facility (PROOF) at its assembly and testing facility. The facilities were inaugurated in the presence of Group Captain and Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla.
STIF is a fully in-house facility for testing reusable rocket stages under flight-like operating conditions. The facility also supports post-flight inspection and requalification of recovered stages. It supports thrust levels from 1 kN to 200 kN, LOX sub-cooling down to 73 K and full-duration burns of up to 150 seconds. The facility will also be used to inspect and requalify recovered stages after flight.
PROOF will enable the in-house manufacturing of pressure vessels — the rocket component that holds gases or liquids at a pressure significantly different from the outside environment. The new facility can produce more than 10 vessels a month, including vessels of up to 3,500 litres and 350 bar.
“The vision of bringing reusability to launch requires us to think beyond a single flight and build the capability to test, recover, inspect and prepare a stage for its next flight. STIF gives us the ability to test complete stages for the duration of their mission and inspect and requalify recovered stages. This is an important capability as we work towards Mission-02,” said Srinath Ravichandran, co-founder and CEO, Agnikul Cosmos.
Grp Capt and astronaut Shukla said, “India’s space programme is entering an exciting phase, with capabilities being built across the country that will enable increasingly ambitious missions. It is encouraging to see Agnikul continue to expand its capabilities in advanced manufacturing and testing.”
Headquartered in Chennai and incubated at IIT Madras, Agnikul Cosmos develops the Agnibaan family of configurable small-lift launch vehicles. In May 2024, it conducted Mission 01, Agnibaan SOrTeD, from its privately built launchpad at Sriharikota.
Agnikul already designs and manufactures its single-piece, 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engines in-house and develops its avionics and other propulsion and vehicle systems.

global-economics-285669d940.headline: US, EU strongly criticise India's tariffs, non-tariff trade barriers
global-economics-285669d940.fulltext:
US, EU strongly criticise India's tariffs, non-tariff trade barriers
Raise concerns over high tariffs, QCOs, digital trade curbs
Listen to This Article
The United States (US) and the European Union (EU), India’s two largest trading partners, have flagged a range of regulatory and non-tariff barriers that they say are undermining the benefits of India’s efforts to open its economy and integrate with global supply chains. 
The concerns, raised during discussions on India’s eighth trade policy review at the World Trade Organization (WTO), include high tariffs, norms meant to protect human, animal and plant health known as sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) measures, technical barriers to trade (TBTs), quality-control orders, restrictions on services and digital trade, local-content requirements and barriers to government procurement. 
The WTO’s trade policy review (TPR) is essentially a peer review of a country’s trade policies. The WTO Secretariat and the country under review prepare separate detailed reports on its trade policies and priorities. 
 
Other WTO members study the reports and submit written questions, seeking explanations for specific tariffs, regulations and other trade barriers. At the review meeting, members raise these issues, while the country responds and explains its policies. India undergoes a TPR once every five years. 
“While we are encouraged by the Indian government's pursuit of trade agreements that will foster transparency and good regulatory practices, India must take additional steps to significantly reduce tariffs, remove unjustified SPS and TBT measures, refrain from imposing barriers to services and digital trade, and roll back regulations that discriminate against foreign exporters and investors,” the US said in its statement, which forms part of the minutes of the latest review available from the WTO.
Also Read
The European Union raised concerns over what it described as unpredictable customs procedures, cumbersome SPS requirements, gaps in protection of intellectual property rights and geographical indications, and narrowing access to government procurement. 
The EU also singled out India’s growing use of Quality Control Orders (QCOs), saying these were creating burdensome conformity-assessment requirements based on domestic standards that deviate from internationally agreed standards. “This risks increasingly insulating the Indian market from the world's economy and reversing the economic progress that we saw over the last years,” it said. 
The EU, however, acknowledged that India has begun addressing the issue. It said a reform process had been initiated following a report by NITI Aayog’s High-Level Committee on QCOs and that full implementation of its recommendations could address many of the concerns.  
The US similarly welcomed India’s recent repeal of some QCOs, but said others continued to affect exports of information and communication technology (ICT) products, medical devices and chemicals. 
It urged India to provide greater opportunities for stakeholder consultation and avoid burdensome testing and certification requirements. India defended its regulatory framework, saying its SPS measures were aimed at facilitating legitimate trade while protecting public health, food safety and biosecurity. 
“Our objective throughout has been to facilitate legitimate trade while safeguarding public health, food safety and biosecurity,” India’s representative to the WTO said, adding that India was committed to transparency through timely WTO notifications, engagement with WTO members and continued strengthening of its SPS systems. 
On technical barriers to trade, India said its QCOs and other technical regulations were designed to meet legitimate objectives, including preventing deceptive practices and protecting human, animal and plant life or health and the environment.
The US also criticised India’s local-content requirements, saying they reduce the competitiveness of imported products across sectors including ICT goods, services, spirits and medical devices. 
It specifically called for India to administer sector-specific measures such as the Import Management System for IT products and licensing and approval procedures for refurbished medical devices in a manner consistent with WTO obligations, without mandatory domestic testing requirements or quantitative restrictions. 
Services remain another area of contention. While recognising India’s recent liberalisation of the insurance and legal sectors, the US said foreign participation remained restricted or prohibited in several other services sectors. 
“In particular, broad restrictions in the electronic payment, retail, and e-commerce sectors appear intended to prevent a level playing field for foreign companies,” the US said, arguing that greater openness would boost foreign participation and help integrate India further into global supply chains. 
The US also welcomed India’s consultations on the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, but urged New Delhi to continue avoiding restrictions on cross-border data flows, including sector-specific data-localisation requirements. 
The EU said the recently concluded India-EU free trade agreement, once ratified, should strengthen bilateral trade and investment ties. But it stressed that implementation would be critical, particularly because the agreement contains ambitious rules on non-tariff barriers. 
“It is also a very ambitious agreement when it comes to the rules, notably on the non-tariff barriers to trade. Implementation will be essential to ensure that the rules we have agreed on paper do materialize on the ground and bring concrete benefits to operators,” the EU said.

global-economics-8833bab144.headline: US bans Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles as trade war escalates
global-economics-8833bab144.fulltext:
The US is banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada, the White House said on Tuesday, as the trade war between the two neighbors and longtime allies escalates.
The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US imports earlier on Tuesday.
Donald Trump also moved to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts as Canada’s retaliatory tariffs took effect and the prime minister, Mark Carney, vowed to speed efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on the United States.
The US president directed the General Services Administration to declare Canadian products ineligible for those contracts until Canada allows “full and fair reciprocity″ for American products.
Carney said on Tuesday that Canada’s strategy was about becoming more independent. “It’s about ensuring that no country can hold us hostage. And that we can live how we want to live.”
The rupture has upended one of the world’s closest relationships. On 22 August, the US imposed 50% tariffs on about 5% of Canadian imports, charging that Canada had unfairly treated the American dairy, alcoholic beverage and auto industries.
The US and Canada have long sparred over trade, particularly Canada’s protected dairy market and the US government’s allegations that it subsidizes producers of softwood lumber. But they remained friends and staunch allies.
Under Trump, US-Canada relations have deteriorated rapidly. In addition to imposing tariffs on Canadian products, Trump has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney came to power in a come-from-behind political victory last year by promising to stand up to him.
Some Canadian provinces have banned the sale of US alcoholic products – a move that prompted the retaliatory US ban on Tuesday.
How the trade war ends could carry consequences far beyond Canada, testing whether a smaller US ally can resist Trump’s economic pressure without being forced to yield.
Earlier on Tuesday, a Canadian official said Ottawa did not intend to change course regardless of whether Trump responded with nothing or what the official called a “nuclear response”.
The government’s strategy will remain focused on building more at home and diversifying trade abroad, the official said.
The tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment, at rates of 15%, 25% or 50%. They cover about $20bn in American goods, roughly 6% of the $333.6bn the United States exported to Canada last year.
Since Canada-US trade talks collapsed 21 August, Trump and his administration have imposed additional tariffs and issued a series of threats and attacks portraying Canada as weak and dependent.
Trump’s trade war and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have fueled anger across the country. Canadians have sharply cut travel to the United States and boycotted US goods, moves Carney praised as signs of national resolve.
Gabriel Brunet, a spokesperson for Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc, said officials from both countries remain in contact even though formal talks have not resumed.

india-d40b2de2b5.headline: Diplomacy tightrope, economic heft test await India at Brics summit
india-d40b2de2b5.fulltext:
The upcoming 18th Brics Summit under India's presidency could turn out to be both an economic lever and a diplomatic endurance test for New Delhi.
At the 11-13 September meetings and on the sidelines, the host country will likely pursue concrete outcomes on crucial agendas, including supply chain resilience, seamless cross-border transactions, energy security, reforms within multilateral bodies, and the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), according to several government officials and experts.
The joint participation of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the summit will also give India an opportunity to rethink its ties with China, push the Global South’s cause and manage the West’s expectations without upsetting its old ally, Russia, officials said. Xi had skipped the previous summit in Rio de Janeiro, while Putin attended it virtually.
“Participation of leaders like Xi, Putin and others in the forthcoming summit in New Delhi is itself a sign of big success, more than concrete outcomes or deliverables,” said Dammu Ravi, India’s former Brics Sherpa and former secretary (economic relations) in the ministry of external affairs (MEA).
New Delhi could also reiterate its message of humanity in the backdrop of continuing wars in West Asia and Ukraine, said a government official on the condition of anonymity.
Brics is a grouping of emerging economies, an acronym of its original members Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. It has since expanded to 11 nations, with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia joining in.
Cross-border cooperation
Government officials said issues such as facilitating greater use of local currencies for cross-border settlements, improving payment connectivity, and reducing the cost of cross-border transactions could see some headway at the summit.
While India hasn’t endorsed the idea of introducing a Brics currency, seen as a challenge to the dollar’s dominance, the country has supported efforts to promote trade settlement in local currencies to raise trade flows.
The officials said discussions are also expected to focus on building resilient and diversified global value chains and strengthening supply-chain cooperation, particularly in strategically important sectors.
Support for micro, small, and medium enterprises, digital trade and trade facilitation are also expected to remain central to the discussions, including cooperation on digitally delivered services, customs and seamless cross-border commerce, they added.
Energy security, access, and equity, in addition to fostering innovation, resilient infrastructure, and capacity-building, are also expected to be in focus, according to two government officials.
Further, in the wake of the war in West Asia and volatility in the energy market, India, through the Global Biofuels Alliance, is expected to push for greater adoption of biofuels and technology transfer, along with investment commitments, added another government official.
The member countries are also expected to come together on new-age technologies, including green hydrogen and carbon capture, utilization and storage, the official added.
Chinese business
The sidelines of the summit could also present an opportunity for India and China to smooth certain bilateral issues, ranging from trade imbalance and visa curbs to investment and market access in China.
Earlier this year, New Delhi allowed overseas entities with up to a 10% Chinese shareholding to invest in the country without prior government approval, as part of a calibrated easing of its foreign direct investment (FDI) policy restrictions. In 2020, New Delhi had tightened its FDI policy, mandating prior government approval for such investments from countries sharing a land border with India.
“India will seek greater access for Indian firms to the Chinese market and the removal of non-tariff barriers,” said a second government official. The Union commerce ministry recently asked industry associations and some trade bodies to provide inputs for this purpose.
Facilitating freer movement of skilled workers and greater Chinese investments in India could be explored in bilateral discussions, the official added.
India’s high goods trade deficit with China has been a sore point. The gap was at $112 billion in financial year 2026, widening from about $99 billion in the previous fiscal. New Delhi has long blamed Beijing for restricting access for Indian exporters, asking the world’s second-largest economy to further open up to Indian goods and services.
Nagesh Kumar, a trade economist and member of the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee, underscored the need to bolster trade cooperation, as envisaged at last month's Brics commerce ministers' meeting, given the disparities among member countries.
“On the one hand, China is the global manufacturing hub running substantial and rising trade surpluses with practically every trade partner; many other Brics members have relatively weaker manufacturing capacities and remain confined to exporting raw commodities, like Ethiopia,” said Kumar.
Cooperation among the member nations would be key to advancing capacity-building and technology transfer “to foster more inclusive and diversified global value chains, helping to share the fruits of trade in a more inclusive manner", Kumar said.
Xi last visited India seven years ago, before the 2020 Galwan clash that had frayed bilateral relations. The Chinese leader will likely be accompanied by a delegation of about 400 officials, compared with fewer than 200 officials the last time in 2019, according to a Reuters report.
The balancing act
New Delhi, experts said, will have to gather all its negotiation skills to pull off an act similar to its 2023 presidency of the G20 grouping, when it managed to produce a joint statement at the end, convincing sparring parties in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to come to some kind of an agreement.
This could be the most challenging task for Indian diplomats and officials this time around as well.
The Brics foreign ministers’ meeting in New Delhi in May didn’t produce a joint statement due to internal divisions, mainly over the ongoing West Asia war, as Iran and the UAE stuck to starkly different stances. This led India to issue a Chair's statement and an outcome document instead, acknowledging the differing positions of certain members.
“A joint statement would be what everyone should be striving for, and any kind of agreement over ways to help end the West Asia conflict would be a key deliverable of the summit and reflect well on its members," said Jayant Dasgupta, former Indian ambassador to the World Trade Organization. "Furthering cooperation where all the members will be benefited, and not a select few, would be another major deliverable.”
Mint's queries emailed to the embassies of the Brics member nations, India’s ministries of external affairs, commerce and industry, petroleum and natural gas, and power, as well as to the Brics 2026 sherpa Sudhakar Dalela on 3 and 4 September remained unanswered.
India last hosted the Brics summit in 2021, when it was virtual due to covid restrictions. The summit had produced some concrete outcomes, including the adoption of a counter-terrorism action plan and support for a Brics digital public goods platform.

india-5eaa9664fd.headline: Concern grows over structures linked with Muslim community in wake of notices, demolition in Uttar Pradesh
india-5eaa9664fd.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-5eaa9664fd.fulltext:
Opposition parties in Uttar Pradesh on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) expressed concern that targeting of mosques and structures linked to the Muslim community will intensify across the State in view of the upcoming Assembly election in a bid to polarise people.
The concern comes against the backdrop of the demolition of a century-old mosque inside the Saharanpur Collectorate complex on September 5 and authorities in Moradabad issuing notice recently to the management of the Mustafa Mosque, describing it as an “unauthorised construction”. The Moradabad Development Authority notice dated August 21, which came into focus on Tuesday, said the construction map of the mosque had not been approved.
“With the Uttar Pradesh election approaching in the next five months, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government is likely to escalate this assault on such structures under the pretext of addressing encroachments. These actions are intended to polarise society along religious lines for electoral gain,” said Afzal Ansari, Lok Sabha MP from Ghazipur and a senior leader Samajwadi Party (SP) leader, calling upon the Supreme Court and High Court to take notice of this “motivated” demolition initiative.
The Congress accused the U.P. government of attempting to instil a sense of “everyday communalism” in the society through such notices. “Development authorities were constituted in Uttar Pradesh after the 1980s... these religious structures are over 100 years old, when no such regulations existed. Structures associated with other communities will also fail the yardstick of the new regulatory framework, but those linked with the Muslim community are being singled out,” said Shahnawaz Alam, Congress national secretary.
‘One-point programme’
Zia ur Rehman Barq, the SP MP from Sambhal, accused the Uttar Pradesh government of pursuing a “one-point programme” focused on mosques, madrasas and graveyards, and criticised officials over the demolition of the mosque in Saharanpur. He alleged that the government was not focusing on inflation, employment, education, health care or services for the poor, and was instead “harassing Muslims” in the belief that it would help it win elections.
Mr. Barq said the Saharanpur mosque was 119 years old and had documents relating to it. He also criticised notices being issued in Sambhal and Moradabad, calling such action “completely wrong”.

world-d4f5ca304d.fulltext:
Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
The loss represents a propaganda victory for Tehran and an awkward setback for Washington’s efforts to project technological superiority
Iran’s capture of a US military underwater drone gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse-engineer the vessel, delivering a setback for the Pentagon and drone maker Anduril.
The US military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands.
The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention.
Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter.
After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then US President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design.
More recently, the US military moved swiftly to prevent Iranian forces from taking possession of uncrewed maritime technology.

UpdateUkraine, Moldova play down Norwegian claim Zelensky’s plane ‘almost hit’ by drone
Officials clarify airspace closure delayed Ukrainian leader’s flight to Oslo following Russian drone intrusion
Ukraine and Moldova on Wednesday played down claims from Norway’s prime minister that a plane carrying President Volodymyr Zelensky was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo.
Jonas Gahr Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK that Zelensky’s plane was “almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova”.
But a source in the Ukrainian presidency described the claim that Zelensky was at risk as “exaggerated”.
“It was an alert in Moldova when a Russian (drone) entered Moldovan and Romanian airspace,” the source told Agence France-Presse.
In Chisinau, government spokesman Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon just after 4.30pm local time due to a Russian drone that entered from the direction of Ukraine.
“The airspace was closed to protect aircraft flying over Moldova at the time: three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result,” he added.

other-interests-abd510cfc1.headline: NASA’s next major telescope might see alien oceans and rainbows
other-interests-abd510cfc1.fulltext:
A NASA telescope in early development should be able to detect light bouncing off the surface of oceans on alien planets, vital information in the hunt for alien life.
The Habitable Worlds Observatory is currently earmarked for launch in the 2040s. It will sport an advanced coronagraph, a device that can block out much of the light emanating from other stars. This will allow us to take images of potentially habitable Earth-like worlds outside our solar system for the first time.
Eleanor Cornish and Tyler Robinson at the University of Arizona have assessed whether the telescope would be able to spot oceans on these planets. Even though its images will be basic, with each world appearing as a single pixel, the pair found that light reflecting off the oceans – known as glint – should be noticeable when the planet is at certain angles around its star.
Advertisement
“Glint signatures can indicate the presence of liquid water on those planets, which is exciting because if we find water, that suggests the planet could be habitable,” says Cornish.
The study shows the glint will be detectable when the angle of the planet relative to its star and Earth, known as its phase angle, is greater than 120 degrees – meaning the light will bounce off the planet towards Earth, rather than out into space. “If it’s at the optimal geometry, we should be able to see it,” says Cornish.
The glint will cause the brightness of the planet to increase slightly. How much the planet brightens in its orbit should tell us how much of the surface is covered by water, revealing whether it is a water world entirely encased in an ocean or partially covered by land like Earth.
Sophia Vaughan at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Germany says it might not just be oceans that the Habitable Worlds Observatory can detect. Other features on the planet, such as clouds, vegetation or even rainbows, might affect the nature of the light that is reflected to Earth. A rainbow would slightly focus the light of the planet, she says, “and you can possibly see that”.
All of this information will be crucial to astronomers as they finalise designs for the Habitable Worlds Observatory in the coming years. “The fact that, maybe in my lifetime, we’ll see the glint of an alien ocean is just incredible,” says Vaughan. “I really hope that we do see it one day.”

other-interests-95cebe28d1.headline: Hypersoft X-ray sources as a low-energy class of luminous cosmic emitter
other-interests-95cebe28d1.fulltext:
Abstract
X-ray binaries, powered by accretion onto black holes, neutron stars or white dwarfs from companion stars, are among the brightest non-explosive beacons in galaxies, outshining the Sun by millions of times in luminosity. Typical X-ray binaries emit primarily above 0.3 keV, whereas cooler sources, peaking in the extreme ultraviolet, remain challenging to detect due to a long-standing observational blind spot. Here we report the discovery of a notable class of luminous, point-like, non-nuclear X-ray objects—hypersoft X-ray sources—that have largely been missed by previous surveys. Detected primarily or exclusively below 0.3 keV, the most luminous examples radiate near 1038 erg s−1 in the narrow X-ray band, with spectral models suggesting even higher bolometric luminosities, most of which emerge in the extreme ultraviolet. They rank among the most energetic sources in galaxies, yet their spectra, which peak in the extreme ultraviolet, evaded earlier detections. We propose that hypersoft sources represent X-ray binaries spanning several physical classes, including accreting white dwarfs or post-nova systems (which are potential progenitors of type Ia supernovae) and systems hosting accreting black holes. Beyond their elusive nature, they may play a crucial role in ionizing gas within galaxies.

beyond-your-beat-c29b90425e.fulltext:
India star nears return with CWC27 on the horizon
Hardik Pandya has been called up to the India A squad, having been out of action from professional cricket since IPL 2026.
All-rounder Hardik Pandya could make his much-awaited return to competitive cricket, subject to fitness clearance, as part of the India A squad for the upcoming three-match one-day series against Australia.
The series, scheduled for October 6 to 11 in Puducherry, could see Pandya return to action after recovering from a leg strain injury he picked up in the lead-up to India’s home series against Afghanistan in June.
Earlier, the 32-year-old also missed out on part of Mumbai Indians’ IPL 2026 campaign owing to back spasms. Pandya’s comeback bodes well for India with the countdown to next year’s ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
CWC27 venues and brand unveiled in a star-studded ceremony
The experienced campaigner hasn’t featured in the 50-over format since the ICC Men’s Champions Trophy last year, where he was part of India’s tournament-winning squad.
Pandya also played a pivotal role in India’s second successive ICC Men’s T20 World Cup triumph earlier this year, finishing the competition with nine wickets in as many games as well as 217 runs.
The all-rounder has had his share of injury bouts, including at the previous Men’s Cricket World Cup in 2023, where he was ruled out midway through the tournament owing to an ankle injury.
Injury blow for India as Hardik Pandya rolls ankle while bowling | CWC23
Having scored 1904 runs and nabbed 91 wickets across his 94 ODI outings for India, Pandya will be crucial to their push for a third world title, having fallen a step short in 2023.
The marquee tournament's 14th edition will see its return to Africa for the first time since 2003, when South Africa and Zimbabwe co-hosted the event alongside Kenya.
Namibia will be co-hosting the tournament for the first time, having staged the ICC Men's Under-19 Cricket World Cup earlier this year.

beyond-your-beat-7010a451d2.headline: Venice Film Festival 2026 Movie Reviews Compilation
beyond-your-beat-7010a451d2.fulltext:
The 2026 Venice Film Festival got underway on Wednesday, September 2, with Oscar-winning English director Danny Boyle’s Ink — starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy — kicking off an 83rd edition that includes films starring the likes of Robert Pattinson, Penelope Cruz & Javier Bardem, Jack Huston & Sofia Boutella, Dakota Johnson, John Malkovich & Sam Rockwell, Alicia Vikander & Susan Sarandon, Nick Nolte and Kate & Rooney Mara in their first movie together.
Along with Ink, this year’s competition lineup includes such buzzy titles seeking awards-season glory as Florian Zeller’s Bunker, Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime, Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, Andrea Pallaoro’s The Echo Chamber, Casey Affleck’s Company and Warner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard.
Studio titles largely are absent this year, but the overall lineup also includes new films by Luca Guadagnino, Paul Schrader and Wim Wenders along with Laura Poitras’ short about ICE protests in Minnesota, and Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace’s doc on the comeback of rock band Oasis.
Watch on Deadline
Check out Deadline’s reviews out of Venice, and keep checking back as we add more. Click on each headline to read our full review.
The Basics of Philosophy
	Section: Out of Competition
Director: Paul Schrader
Cast: Jack Huston, Sofia Boutella, Daniel Zovalto, Bill Pullman, Dana Delany, Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman, Elizabeth Petruso, Santiago Cabrera, Trevor Dolden, Richard Gere
Deadline’s takeaway: With this introspective character study, Schrader continues to making the kind of grownup films we rarely get to see anymore, outside of Europe at least. He never presents easy answers in his movies — same with this deep dive into the philosophy of life and the key question we can ask of many Schrader characters, “Can we change?” — PH
Bucking Fastard
	Section: Competition
Director-screenwriter: Werner Herzog
Cast: Kate Mara, Rooney Mara, Orlando Bloom, Domhnall Gleeson
Deadline’s takeaway: Although it appears to start with a tone of gentle mockery, there’s something quite sweet and generous at work beneath the stylized strangeness of the tale of two sisters played by Rooney and Kate Mara, a tone that Werner Herzog has never really struck before in his fiction work, with the possible exception of 2019’s Family Romance LLC. — DW
	
Bunker
	Section: Competition
Director-screenwriter: Florian Zeller
Cast: Javier Bardem, Penélope Cruz, Stephen Graham, Paul Dano, Patrick Schwarzenegger
Deadline’s takeaway: Florian Zeller casts real-life husband and wife Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz in this rich and fascinating film to blur the lines between reality and fiction, using the marriage of their Miguel and Sofia to examine not just the crisis within it but all around them — fear of the future, environmental threats, inequality, individualism, post-pandemic isolation and other themes on the filmmaker’s mind. — PH
Company
	Section: Competition
Director: Casey Affleck
Cast: Nick Nolte, Ben Mendelsohn, Adelaide Clemens, Scott McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, Caylee Cowan, Atticus Affleck, Indiana Affleck
Deadline’s takeaway: Ben Affleck as a filmmaker seems most influenced by films in which he starred — his Oscar-winning role in Manchester By the Sea, The Assassination of Jesse James By the Coward Robert Ford and David Lowery’s A Ghost Story to cite three that ask us to go with flow, slow down and take it all in. That is how it felt watching Company, a movie that asks us to simply watch and listen, to let it roll over us, and perhaps to discover the meaning of the words we say to each other. — PH
Father Joe
	Section: Venice Open – Out Of Competition
Director: Barthélémy Grossmann
Cast: Kiefer Sutherland, Ever Anderson, Al Pacino, Michael Rispoli
Deadline’s takeaway: Amazingly, Al Pacino is about the only thing that isn’t over the top here, generously giving center stage to Kiefer Sutherland in a role that’s fun, unbelievable — and sometimes unbelievably funny. Is it any good? Who knows. It’s certainly the most balls-out, no-f*cks-given rock ’n’ roll phenomenon to hit the Lido this year — DW
The Girl with the Leica
	Section: Orizzonti
Director: Alina Marazzi
Cast: Emilia Schüle, Aaron Altaras, Luna Wedler, Lucas Englander, Thomas Schubert, Sebastian Schneider, Idan Weiss, Lia von Blarer, Hans-Christian Hegewald, Jeremy Mockridge, Joel Basman
Deadline’s takeaway: The jazzed-up, unconventional biopic of the late photojournalist Gerda Taro asks questions about the the fine line between bravery and ego in the process of bringing back dispatches from the front line, but its structure over-complicates a simple yet quite profound meditation on an artist’s identity and legacy. — DW
Ink
	Section: Competition
Director: Danny Boyle
Cast: Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, Claire Foy, Jonathan Hyde, Lucy Russell, Abigail Amin, Bertie Carvel, Brian Gleeson, Christopher Fulford, Patrick Kennedy, Blake Harrison, Georgie Henley
Deadline’s takeaway: Danny Boyle with his whip-smart, in-your-face stye is the perfect filmmaker to bring this world set in 1969 London to life as the brash if trash visionary Rupert Murdoch and his hand-picked editor-in-chief launch what would become a new era of tabloid journalism, changing the media world for better or worse in the process. Here all the cylinders are firing, and it is thrilling stuff indeed. — PH
Joie de Vivre
	Section: Venice Open – Out of Competition
Director: Luca Guadagnino
Deadline’s takeaway: Luca Guadagnino’s 426-minute docu-essay about Italian maestro Bernardo Bertolucci is the endurance test of this year’s festival. Surprisingly, however, watched in two sittings, it is less of an ordeal than it might appear, partly thanks to Guadagnino’s forthright views. Bertolucci, though, often gets pushed aside by Guadagnino and company, even while the speakers onscreen complain that Bertolucci was often pushed aside as a filmmaker. — DW
	
Musk
	Section: Out of Competition
Director: Alex Gibney
Deadline’s takeaway: The documentary, which might be Alex Gibney’s most important, depicts the world’s richest man as petty, narcissistic, megalomaniacal, cruel and detached from humans at a personal level while purporting to want to save humanity by colonizing Mars. In other words, it gives Elon the takedown he richly deserves. — MC
Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger
	Section: Venice Open – Out of Competition
Directors: Dylan Southern, Will Lovelace
With: Liam Gallagher, Noah Gallagher
Deadline’s takeaway: The great mystery about why Noel and Liam Gallagher put aside their differences for a heavily promoted multimillion-dollar world stadium tour is never really addressed in this more-than-feature-length documentary. Instead, the directors look at what came out of it for the estranged brothers, offering an insider’s view one of the most crazily oversubscribed reunion tours of all time. — DW
Place to Be
	Section: Out of Competition
Director: Kornél Mundruczó
Cast: Ellen Burstyn, Taika Waititi, Pamela Anderson, David Wenham, Lena Waithe, Murray Bartlett
Deadline’s takeaway: Ellen Burstyn, Taika Waititi and 25 pigeons all contribute to the success of this lovely little film that deserves to find its audience, if only to rediscover something we already knew: that Ellen Burstyn is an acting treasure. — PH
Possible Love
	Section: Competition
Director: Lee Chang-dong
Cast: Jeon Do-Yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-Jeung
Deadline’s takeaway: As you might expect from this master filmmaker, the story takes time to develop, and at nearly three hours it takes a little too long here. But the cast of top South Korean actors here is well chosen, and they deliver Lee Chang-dong’s vision on the screen in this handsomely filmed and pertinent film. — PH
Primetime
	Section: Competition
Director: Lance Oppenheim
Cast: Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers, Anna Faris
Deadline’s takeaway: Primetime is a film about the way populism fuels moral decadence — but in such a subtle way that its proponents don’t realize it. They usually do, however, when what goes around comes around, which is very much the moral of the story here. Delivering a performance described as a mixture of Jerry Maguire and Count Dracula, Robert Pattinson may finally be entering the Christian Bale period of his career. — DW
The Spiral
	Section: Competition
Director: Paolo Strippoli
Cast: Jasmine Trinca, Romana Maggiora Vergano, Adriano Giannini, Valeria Bruni Tedeschi
Deadline’s takeaway: Does Paolo Strippoli’s unashamedly commercial horror-thriller reinvent the wheel? No, it doesn’t. But instead of lecturing us about the parlous state of the world today, he is happy to give us a grand guignol morality play that tells us not so much that we’re doomed but reminds us that it’s the things that we might yet do that may throw our lives off-track. — DW
Wild Horse Nine
	Section: Competition
Director: Martin McDonagh
Cast: John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas, Tom Waits, Parker Posey
Deadline’s takeaway: John Malkovich gives a career performance in a perfect if unexpected casting. This so-called “buddy movie” of a wildly different stripe easily is one of the year’s best films, and in its own peculiar way the most spiritual. Martin McDonagh now is 5-for-5 as a writer-director. — PH

AIIS Research Fellowships 2026–27: Applications Open for Scholars Conducting Research on India
The American Institute of Indian Studies (AIIS) has opened applications for its 2026–27 Research Fellowship Competition, offering scholars an opportunity to undertake research connected to India. The programme provides three fellowship pathways: the Junior Research Fellowship, AIIS NEH Senior Research Fellowship, and Early Career Scholar Travel Fellowship.
The application deadline for the 2026 AIIS Fellowship Competition is November 19, 2026. Applicants are encouraged to carefully review the requirements for their selected fellowship, as each category has distinct eligibility criteria and application instructions.
Fellowship Opportunities
The Junior Research Fellowship is designed for doctoral students conducting research in Indian Studies. Non-US citizens may apply provided they are enrolled as doctoral students at a US institution.
The AIIS NEH Senior Research Fellowship supports established scholars pursuing advanced research related to India, while the Early Career Scholar Travel Fellowship provides travel support for eligible early-career researchers.
Applicants who are not affiliated with an AIIS member institution are also welcome to apply.
Junior Fellowship Application Requirements
Junior Fellowship applicants must submit a comprehensive application containing biographical and scholarly information, the proposed project title and discipline, a 350-word project abstract, and a 150-word fieldwork justification statement.
The application must also include a short CV of no more than two pages and unofficial transcripts from undergraduate and graduate institutions.
Applicants are required to submit a project statement of no more than 2,100 words explaining the proposed research. The statement should clearly present the research questions and rationale, explain the project’s significance and relationship to existing scholarship, outline the research methodology, and provide a timetable for completing the project. The word count must be included at the end of the statement.
A 1–3 page bibliography must demonstrate how the proposed research engages with relevant existing scholarship.
Applicants must also provide a personal statement of no more than 350 words, offering additional context that is not addressed elsewhere in the application. This may include relevant experiences, inspiration, challenges, or biographical information.
Applicants who previously applied unsuccessfully for an AIIS Junior Fellowship with the same project may optionally submit a revision statement of up to 500 words, explaining how the new application has been improved.
A financial aid statement is also required.
How Applications Are Evaluated
AIIS evaluates applications through a rigorous two-round review process. In the first round, reviewers assess information submitted through the application form, including the CV, project abstract, and fieldwork justification.
Finalists proceed to the second round, where reviewers assess the project statement, bibliography, personal statement, and revision statement where applicable.
The selection committee considers four major factors: the excellence and merit of the project, project design and methodology, the candidate’s academic or professional record, and financial need.
Because reviewers come from different disciplines within Indian Studies, applicants are strongly encouraged to explain their research in clear language that can be understood by scholars outside their specific field. Excessive jargon should be avoided.
Important Fellowship Conditions
All AIIS Fellows, regardless of citizenship, must obtain a Certificate of Affiliation with an Indian research centre. US citizens must obtain either a research visa or, where applicable, special research permission for OCI cardholders. AIIS assists Fellows in obtaining the necessary documentation for research in India.
Fellowship recipients must provide proof of travel before receiving their award. Travel must generally take place within two years of selection.
AIIS has limited fellowship funding. Applicants who receive another research fellowship or scholarship exceeding $10,000 cannot hold both awards simultaneously and may be required to relinquish the AIIS fellowship so that the funding can be awarded to another scholar.
Incomplete applications will not be considered.
Mentoring and Application Support
AIIS offers a mentoring service for Junior Fellowship applicants who do not have faculty advisers with South Asia expertise at their home institutions. This service can provide valuable guidance to applicants developing their research proposals.
AIIS will also host a successful application webinar on October 9, 2026, designed to provide practical guidance on preparing a competitive fellowship application. Applicants can also review webinars from previous years and examine examples of successful Junior Fellowship project statements.
Application Deadline and Submission
The application deadline for the 2026 AIIS Fellowship Competition is November 19, 2026. Prospective applicants should begin preparing their research statements, supporting documents, transcripts, bibliography, and financial information well before the deadline.
Junior Fellowship applicants can access the application through the official AIIS application portal. Finalists are expected to be announced by mid-March, with fellowship recipients announced by early May.
The AIIS Research Fellowship Competition represents a significant opportunity for scholars seeking to deepen research on India while developing rigorous, field-based scholarship. Applicants with strong research proposals, clearly defined methodologies, relevant academic or professional records, and demonstrated financial need are encouraged to prepare carefully and submit complete applications before the deadline.

opportunities-1599f03e71.headline: NFSU's IDDRC to host India Digital ADR Summit 2026 on AI, cybersecurity and digital evidence: Registrations open
opportunities-1599f03e71.fulltext:
The India Digital ADR Summit 2026, organised by the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU), Gandhinagar, through its International Digital Dispute Resolution Centre (IDDRC), is set to be held on 12 and 13 September 2026 at NFSU, Gandhinagar, Gujarat. The two-day summit will bring together judges, senior advocates, arbitrators, mediators, legal scholars, policymakers, industry leaders, technology experts and researchers to deliberate on the evolving landscape of Dispute Resolution in the digital era.
About International Digital Dispute Resolution Centre
The IDDRC is a specialised institutional initiative of the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU), Gandhinagar established to advance technology-enabled, efficient and secure dispute resolution. The Centre operates through a professional Secretariat, formally notified procedural rules and a curated panel of experts and practitioners.
Board of Governors
The IDDRC is guided by an eminent Board of Governors comprising distinguished members of the judiciary and legal profession:
- 
Justice Anil R. Dave — Former Judge, Supreme Court of India; President, IDDRC
- 
Justice Rajesh Bindal — Former Judge, Supreme Court of India
- 
Justice M. R. Shah — Former Judge, Supreme Court of India
- 
Justice Sonia Gokani — Former Chief Justice, Gujarat High Court
- 
Justice P. P. Bhatt — Former Judge, Gujarat High Court
- 
Gourab Banerji— Senior Advocate and President, Arbitration Bar of India
- 
Ratan Singh — Senior Advocate and Chairman, Society of Construction Law, India
About India Digital ADR Summit
The Summit provides a collaborative forum to explore how digital innovation is transforming arbitration, mediation, and access to justice, while also addressing the legal, ethical, procedural, cybersecurity, and institutional challenges arising from the increasing use of technology in dispute resolution.
Summit Vision
The Summit seeks to foster meaningful dialogue on the future of Alternative Dispute Resolution by promoting innovation, collaboration, and thought leadership within an increasingly digital and interconnected legal ecosystem.
Key Themes
The Summit focuses on emerging and critical areas in Digital ADR, including:
- 
Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) and technology-enabled dispute resolution;
- 
Artificial Intelligence and its applications in arbitration and mediation;
- 
Digital evidence and evidentiary challenges;
- 
Procedural fairness and due process in digital proceedings;
- 
Cybersecurity, data protection, and confidentiality;
- 
Cross-border digital dispute resolution; and
- 
The broader impact of technological innovation on access to justice.
Round Table Discussions
A key feature of the Summit is its interactive round table discussions, led by eminent experts and practitioners. These sessions facilitate the exchange of practical experiences, academic perspectives, and policy insights on contemporary developments and emerging challenges in Digital ADR.
Research and Knowledge Creation
The Summit aims to document and consolidate the deliberations and insights emerging from its sessions, thereby identifying research themes and areas for further scholarly engagement. This knowledge-building initiative is intended to contribute to sustained academic discourse and future scholarship in the field of technology-enabled dispute resolution.
Collaborative Platform
The Summit serves as a platform for strengthening collaboration among judicial officers, legal practitioners, arbitrators, mediators, academics, policymakers, and institutional leaders. By bringing together diverse stakeholders, it seeks to foster meaningful partnerships and encourage innovation, policy development, capacity building, and excellence in dispute resolution.
Key Discussions
The first day of the summit will commence with an Inaugural on “Artificial Intelligence in Arbitration: Enhancing Decision-Making Without Replacing Human Judgment.”
This will be followed by a panel discussion on “India as a Global Arbitration Hub: Building a Competitive and Technology-Enabled Arbitration Ecosystem.”
The round table will focus on “Building India’s Digital ADR Architecture: Institutional, Regulatory and Technological Priorities.”
The day will conclude with discussions on “Mediation after the Mediation Act, 2023: From Statutory Framework to Institutional Practice,” examining the transition from the statutory framework to its practical and institutional implementation.
The second day will feature a panel discussion on “Emergency Arbitration & Interim Relief: Court–Tribunal Interface”, followed by a discussion on “The Enforcement Gap: Setting Aside, Recognition & Enforcement of Awards.” The summit will conclude with a closing ceremony.
A Forum for Digital Justice
The summit is envisioned as a collaborative platform for meaningful dialogue between the judiciary, legal profession, academia, government, industry and technology sectors. It aims to facilitate the exchange of practical experiences, academic perspectives and policy insights while fostering greater collaboration in the field of digital dispute resolution.
Through interactive panel discussions and round-table deliberations, the summit will provide participants an opportunity to engage with emerging developments in AI, Online Dispute Resolution, digital evidence, cybersecurity and regulatory frameworks, while gaining perspectives from practitioners and decision-makers working in contemporary dispute resolution.
With technology increasingly influencing the manner in which disputes are managed and resolved, the India Digital ADR Summit 2026 is poised to provide an important forum for examining the opportunities and challenges accompanying this transformation and for considering the future architecture of technology-enabled ADR in India and beyond.
For more details about the India Digital ADR Summit 2026, including the detailed programme, speakers, registration information and other event particulars, please refer to the official event brochure.
